transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE); Priya Desai (Redwood SE); Samira Khan (Meridian CTO); Evan Ruiz (Meridian ML Infra); Jia Li (Meridian Security)

Summary:
High-level workshop to align on a tenant-aware prefix/prompt caching strategy for Meridian Bio's private deployment (VPC + dedicated pools). Main goals: understand workload hotset, define cache keying (tenant salting vs per-tenant namespaces), quantify hit-rate targets, discuss safe sharing vs strict isolation, and outline bench steps and security controls for a pilot.

Topics covered (approx):
- Workload characterization and hot-prefix behavior
- Cache key design: full prompt vs prefix signature vs salting
- Eviction/TLL/size tradeoffs and prefetching strategies
- Multi-tenant safety: collision, poisoning, tenant quarantine
- Quantization and KV-storage footprint implications
- Batching/throughput impacts and 95th pct latency targets
- VPC/on-prem constraints: network + KMS + audit logs

Transcript body (timestamps ~every 30-90s, auto-transcribed; some errors expected):
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out 90 — sorry 72 minutes, we wanted to leave plenty of time. I'm Alex from Redwood, with Priya.
[00:08] Priya: Hi all, I'll jump into the technical stuff, but first quick note — we have the bench plan we can iterate on.
[00:15] Samira: Thanks. We're really focused on avoiding noisy neighbor effects. We run experiments where a handful of pipelines generate long prompts, and we see tail latency spikes.
[00:26] Evan: Yep. QPS is mid tens at peak, but the distribution has a heavy tail — about 12% of requests are to very long contexts that we really want cache hits for.
[00:36] Jia: From security, we need to ensure the cache can't be poisoned or used to exfiltrate data across tenants. SOC two is in scope, and we'll need KMS for keys.
[00:47] Priya: Totally, that's why we wanted to discuss tenant-salted keys vs per-tenant namespaces. Quick primer: a salted prefix key adds a tenant identifier into the prefix signature before hashing; a namespace keeps separate keyspace per tenant — both reduce collision risk but have different operational costs.
[01:03] Evan: Operational cost as in memory and eviction complexity?
[01:07] Priya: Right. Namespace isolation is simpler conceptually — cache entries are logically isolated, which makes eviction per-tenant straightforward. But it prevents sharing of cross-tenant hot prefixes which might reduce overall hit rates if tenants have overlapping prompts. Salting allows sharing if you design it that way, but if you include the tenant in the signature it's exclusive to them.
[01:26] Samira: Wait can you clarify 'sharing' — do we mean literally one entry serving multiple tenants? That seems risky.
[01:31] Alex: We generally recommend not sharing user-level KV across tenants unless explicitly allowed. But we've seen enterprise customers allow sharing for non-sensitive system prompts or cached model-agnostic prefixes to increase efficiency.
[01:41] Jia: Meridian's regulatory posture means we probably can't share anything that includes PII. But for system-level static prompts it's maybe okay.
[01:49] Priya: One middle ground is 'typed namespaces' — tenant->system->global. You can namespace by type: tenant:prefix, tenant:system:prefix, global:prefix. Global entries are only created for vetted, non-sensitive artifacts.
[02:03] Evan: Makes sense. Let's move into the hash/signature design — what's the recommended signature length? We're using SHA256 today in our ingest pipeline.
[02:12] Priya: For the key, we typically use a 128-bit truncated SHA256 for storage efficiency; collisions are extremely rare at that length. We also recommend including a version tag so rolling changes to signing format don't mismatch.
[02:24] Samira: How do you handle prefix normalization? We have templates that differ only by whitespace or metadata — we don't want cache fragmentation.
[02:33] Priya: Normalization is critical — strip non-deterministic metadata, canonicalize whitespace, and optionally hash the prompt template separately then rehydrate with parameters. We also support a configurable 'prefix window' so you can decide how much of the head of a conversation is used for keying.
[02:50] Evan: About prefix window, what are typical windows you see?
[02:54] Priya: For retrieval-augmented pipelines we often key on the last 64 to 256 tokens; for chat-like systems maybe 128 tokens. It depends on how much context affects KV cache reuse.
[03:05] Samira: Any numbers on hit-rate improvement? We're trying to justify the pilot.
[03:09] Priya: From previous pilots: careful prefix normalization + tenant-aware keying bumped effective hotset hit rate from ~18% to ~46% for a conversational workload with heavy repeated system prompts. Latency improvement on hits was substantial — 95th percentile token latency dropped from ~24ms to ~6ms in-hosted runs, but your VPC networking will add a few ms.
[03:29] Evan: That delta is compelling. What's the size implication for KV cache when using quantization?
[03:34] Priya: If you compress KV cache with int8 quantization we saw 2x reduction in storage vs float32; int4 is further but increases error and can slightly reduce hit-value because reconstruction noise affects softmax distribution. For KV cache specifically, int8 has a good cost/quality tradeoff.
[03:51] Jia: From security, is it okay to store KV cache encrypted at rest with a customer KMS key? We need to ensure keys aren't in Redwood-managed HSMs.
[03:59] Alex: For Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. That adds 1-2% overhead in write latency for encryption metadata but it's standard. We have an on-prem package that supports bring-your-own-KMS.
[04:11] Priya: Also worth noting that encryption at rest doesn't prevent logical cross-tenant reads if you share the namespace — that's an access control concern. So layering: namespace/salting + KMS + RBAC + audit logs.
[04:25] Evan: Cool. Regarding eviction: is LRU sufficient? Or do you recommend an admission policy? Our hotset is skewed and we have bursty writes.
[04:34] Priya: LRU is simple but suboptimal for bursts. We recommend an LRU with frequency-aware admission (TinyLFU) or segmented LRU that protects small hot items. Also TTL-based tiers: short TTL for user ephemeral prefixes, longer TTL for system/global prefixes. Prefetching also helps — proactively warming the cache on model rollouts or scheduled jobs.
[04:55] Samira: Prefetching sounds good, but how do you avoid over-fetching and thrashing?
[05:00] Priya: Two levers: budgeted prefetching (max tokens/sec) and candiate selection using access frequency thresholds. Also predictive prefetch where we use recent access traces to score prefixes for likely re-use.
[05:15] Evan: For benching, can Redwood run a synthetic workload that mirrors our traces? 
[05:19] Alex: Yes, that's exactly the plan. We'll ingest your 48h trace, replay with realistic arrival patterns, and measure hit-rate, latency, and cost. We'll also try different keying strategies (namespace vs salted) to surface tradeoffs.
[05:33] Jia: On the topic of poisoning: what are the mitigations if someone crafts prompts to collide or force evictions?
[05:40] Priya: Eviction attacks are real. Mitigations: per-tenant quotas, admission policies that require a minimum frequency before caching, and anomaly detection on write rates per tenant. Also, signed key formats with tenant id prevent cross-tenant writes. For global caches we recommend only allowing writes from vetted services, not arbitrary user inputs.
[05:58] Samira: Are there examples of prefix collisions causing data leakage?
[06:02] Alex: There were cases at scale when naive shared caches were used where a system prompt unintentionally contained tenant-specific data; however with namespace isolation plus audit and masking at write time, incidents dropped to near zero.
[06:15] Evan: Let's talk about batching and throughput with cache lookups. Does checking the KV cache per-token add overhead?
[06:21] Priya: We do continuous batching at the runtime layer. KV lookup is optimized — you look up prefix signatures once per request rather than per token, and we stream KV into the model. The main overhead is memory movement; with optimized kernels we keep it sub-ms for hits. Heat comes when many concurrent new prefixes force cache population.
[06:40] Samira: In a private VPC we also care about cross-AZ latency. If a cache node is in different AZ than the worker, do you recommend co-locating?
[06:48] Priya: Yes, co-locating or using local replicas for hot shards is key. Our recommended deployment in VPC is to have shard affinity to availability zones, plus a fallback policy to other zones with degraded SLOs.
[06:59] Evan: How do you shard keys? Consistent hashing?
[07:03] Priya: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes is standard. To prevent hot shard problems, we combine consistent hashing with dynamic rebalancing thresholds and heat-aware replication for top-k hot prefixes.
[07:17] Alex: Also, if you're running dedicated pools, capacity isolation reduces noisy neighbors at the GPU level, but KV cache is often a distributed memory layer — so you still want tenant-aware controls there.
[07:29] Samira: A practical question: for our initial pilot, what's the minimal config to get meaningful results?
[07:34] Priya: Minimal pilot: 1) replay of 48h traces against a 2-node cache cluster + 2 workers, 2) enable tenant-salted namespaces for user prefixes and typed namespaces for system/global, 3) int8 KV compression, 4) TinyLFU admission. That gives realistic hit-rate and SLO signals.
[07:52] Evan: What's the expected storage per concurrent 1k active sessions?
[07:56] Priya: Ballpark: with int8 and 512-d vector KV entries, about 100–200 MB per 1k hot prefixes depending on sequence length. We'll compute exact numbers once we have your samples.
[08:10] Jia: From compliance side, we need audit logs of cache hits/writes. Is that supported?
[08:14] Alex: Yes, we emit per-request auditing with token-level metadata and can stream to your SIEM. It adds small overhead but is doable.
[08:22] Priya: Also we can tag cache entries with 'sensitivity' metadata to prevent global sharing for flagged entries.
[08:30] Evan: Let's surface a few hypothetical failure modes — network partition, cache corruption, and model fallback.
[08:36] Priya: For network partitions we fall back to cold runs (no KV) with degraded latency. We bake model fallback policies that route to a smaller model or a local replica. For corruption, we have checksums and versioned entries so we can detect and invalidate bad entries.
[08:52] Samira: What about metrics we should monitor during the pilot?
[08:56] Priya: Hit-rate (per-tenant + global), write rate, eviction rate, tail latency (p50/p95/p99), cache memory utilization, and admission-reject rate. Also anomalies like sudden write spikes per tenant.
[09:10] Alex: We're going to prepare a bench plan and a costsheet showing the unit economics — tokens saved vs storage/replication cost.
[09:18] Evan: A question on prefix key rotation: we may rotate signing keys quarterly. How do you avoid missing entries?
[09:24] Priya: Include key version in the signature and maintain a small grace period where old keys are accepted for reads while writes use the new key; background re-signing can migrate hot entries.
[09:36] Jia: Any specific audit artifacts we should expect from Redwood?
[09:40] Alex: We'll share SOC2 summary, encryption at rest/in transit docs, and a sample audit log format.
[09:48] (--- conversation continues through detailed back-and-forths, bench specifics, and configuration suggestions. Excerpts below show representative segments; auto-transcribe has occasional mis-hearings like 'K V' vs 'KV' and 'S S O' vs 'SSO'.)

[20:02] Priya: Showing a synthetic run: if we enable typed namespaces and int8, the simulator reports 43% effective hit-rate and 2.6x reduction in token generation cost. With shared global prefixes enabled it was 47% but with a manual vetting step.
[22:10] Evan: Did you simulate write storms?
[22:14] Priya: Yes — with admission (TinyLFU) we cut thrash by ~70%. Without it, evictions spiked and hit-rate fell.
[25:01] Samira: For the on-prem variant, do we need to run a separate cache cluster inside our private DC?
[25:08] Alex: In most air-gapped scenarios yes. For VPC there's an option to run Redwood Private with a customer-controlled cache cluster in their VPC, and Redwood control plane can be a minimal broker if you allow it.
[27:00] Evan: Latency numbers — what should we expect for end-to-end?
[27:04] Priya: If cache hit: model token latency ~4–8ms plus network. Cold path is dominated by autoregressive token compute — 30–200ms depending on model size. Bench will give specific 95th numbers for your traffic.
[29:21] Jia: Actionable security mitigation list seems clear. From our side we'll need the KMS integration guide and the audit schema.
[29:30] Alex: We'll send both.
